question: A tank endorsement is required for a Class A or B CDL driver who wants to haul liquid or liquid gas in a tank meeting which capacity description?
choice_a: Individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more
choice_b: Individual rated capacity of more than 1,000 gallons only
choice_c: Aggregate rated capacity of more than 119 gallons only, regardless of individual tank size
choice_d: Any tank used to haul liquid, regardless of size
explanation: A tank endorsement is required when hauling liquid or liquid gas in a tank or tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate rated capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-1

question: On all tank vehicles, what is the most important item to check for during inspection?
explanation: The manual states that on all tank vehicles, the most important item to check for is leaks, both under and around the vehicle.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-1

question: Why should you inspect a tanker before loading, unloading, or driving it?
choice_b: To make sure it is safe to carry the liquid or gas and safe to drive
choice_c: It is only required for annual state inspection, not every trip
explanation: Inspecting the tanker before loading, unloading, or driving makes sure the vehicle is safe to carry the liquid or gas and safe to drive.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-1

question: If your tank vehicle is equipped with a vapor recovery kit, grounding and bonding cables, and an emergency shut-off system, what must you confirm during inspection?
choice_a: That they are painted a visible color
choice_c: That they have been removed for the trip
choice_d: Only that the fire extinguisher is present; the rest is optional
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to make sure special purpose equipment such as vapor recovery kits, grounding and bonding cables, emergency shut-off systems, and a built-in fire extinguisher all work.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-1

question: Why are liquid tankers especially prone to rolling over?
choice_a: They have a high center of gravity that makes them top-heavy
choice_b: They have unusually low ground clearance
choice_c: They are always overloaded beyond legal limits
explanation: High center of gravity means much of the load's weight is carried high up off the road, making the vehicle top-heavy and easy to roll over; tests have shown tankers can turn over at the speed limits posted for curves.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: Because tankers can roll over even at the posted speed limit for a curve, what should a tank vehicle driver do?
choice_a: Maintain the posted speed exactly through the curve
choice_b: Take highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves well below the posted speed
choice_c: Accelerate through curves to reduce time spent turning
choice_d: Only slow down when the tank is empty
explanation: The manual advises taking highway curves and on-ramp/off-ramp curves well below the posted speeds, since tanker rollover tests show they can turn over at those posted speeds.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: What is "liquid surge" in a tank vehicle?
choice_a: Static electricity building up inside the tank
choice_b: Movement of the liquid in a partially filled tank that can push the vehicle when the wave hits the end of the tank
choice_c: The expansion of liquid as it warms
explanation: Liquid surge results from movement of the liquid in partially filled tanks; when the wave hits the end of the tank, it tends to push the truck in the direction the wave is moving.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: On a slippery surface such as ice, what danger can liquid surge create when a tank vehicle comes to a stop?
choice_a: The wave of liquid can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection
choice_b: The tank will automatically vent excess pressure
choice_d: The trailer landing gear will collapse
explanation: If the truck is on a slippery surface such as ice, the surge wave can shove a stopped truck out into an intersection.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: When loading or unloading smaller tanks separated by bulkheads, what must a driver pay attention to?
choice_a: Weight distribution, so as not to put too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle
choice_c: The order in which each bulkhead was manufactured
choice_d: The temperature rating printed on each bulkhead
explanation: Some liquid tanks are divided into smaller tanks by bulkheads; when loading and unloading them, the driver must pay attention to weight distribution and avoid putting too much weight on the front or rear of the vehicle.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: What do baffled liquid tanks contain that helps control forward-and-backward liquid surge?
choice_b: Bulkheads with holes that let the liquid flow through
choice_c: A pressurized air cushion between compartments
explanation: Baffled liquid tanks have bulkheads in them with holes that let the liquid flow through, which helps control forward and backward liquid surge -- though side-to-side surge can still occur and cause a rollover.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: Un-baffled ("smooth bore") tanks, often used to haul food products like milk, have nothing inside to slow the flow of liquid. What does this mean for the driver?
choice_a: Forward-and-back surge is very strong, requiring extra caution when starting and stopping
choice_b: The tank cannot legally be filled past half capacity
choice_c: They are exempt from the CDL tank vehicle endorsement requirement
choice_d: They automatically require a hazardous materials endorsement
explanation: Un-baffled tankers have nothing inside to slow the flow of liquid, so forward-and-back surge is very strong; the manual advises being extremely cautious, especially when starting and stopping.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: What is "outage" in the context of loading a cargo tank?
choice_a: A temporary power failure during unloading
choice_b: The room deliberately left unfilled in a tank so the liquid can expand as it warms
choice_c: The amount of fuel used to complete a delivery
choice_d: A report filed after a spill
explanation: You must never load a cargo tank totally full because liquids expand as they warm, and you must leave room for the expanding liquid -- this is called outage; different liquids require different amounts of outage.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: When deciding how much of a dense liquid, such as some acids, to load into a tank, which factors must a driver take into account?
choice_b: The amount the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits
choice_c: Only the color of the liquid
choice_d: Only the distance to the destination
explanation: A full tank of dense liquid may exceed legal weight limits, so the amount to load depends on how much the liquid will expand in transit, the weight of the liquid, and legal weight limits.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-2

question: Because of the tank's high center of gravity and liquid surge, how should a driver start, slow down, and stop a tank vehicle?
choice_a: As quickly as possible to minimize time exposed on the road
choice_b: Very smoothly, and with smooth turns and lane changes
choice_d: In a series of short, hard braking pulses
explanation: Because of the high center of gravity and the surge of the liquid, a tank vehicle driver must start, slow down, and stop very smoothly, and make smooth turns and lane changes.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-3

question: What braking technique helps control surge when bringing a tank vehicle to a stop?
choice_a: Releasing the brakes early so the surge dissipates before stopping
choice_b: Keeping a steady pressure on the brakes and not releasing too soon
choice_c: Pumping the brakes rapidly and repeatedly
choice_d: Using only the engine brake and never the service brake
explanation: To control surge, keep a steady pressure on the brakes, do not release too soon when coming to a stop, and brake far in advance while increasing your following distance.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-3

question: Which statement about tank vehicle stopping distance is correct according to the manual?
choice_a: Full tank vehicles always stop faster than empty ones
choice_b: Wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones
choice_c: Stopping distance is unaffected by road surface conditions
choice_d: Empty tank vehicles always stop faster than fully loaded ones
explanation: The manual warns that wet roads double the normal stopping distance, and empty tank vehicles may take longer to stop than full ones.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-3

question: On a tank trailer, what can happen if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid?
choice_d: Nothing significant; tank trailers cannot skid
explanation: Over steering, over accelerating, or over braking can cause a skid; on tank trailers, if the drive wheels or trailer wheels begin to skid, the vehicle may jackknife.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 8 - Tank Vehicles, p. 8-3
